newsitem.title: KUWAIT: New strike on Iraq possible, Perry says.
newsitem.headline: New strike on Iraq possible, Perry says.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Sunday further strikes on Gulf War foe Iraq were still a possibility and asked Kuwait to allow in 5,000 more U.S. troops to boost American might in the oil-rich region.

Perry told a news conference in Kuwait that the United States "will take whatever action is necessary" to enforce an expanded southern Iraqi no-fly zone up to the 33rd parallel and to protect U.S. pilots patrolling it.
"We will not tolerate this threat to our pilots," Perry said, adding Washington stood "shoulder to shoulder" with Saudi Arabia and Kuwait during heightened tension with Baghdad.
Perry is on a visit to the Gulf to try to rally the Gulf War alliance against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein following Iraqi missile attacks against U.S. planes patrolling the no-fly zone.
Security at the airport news conference was tight. U.S. security men milled around Perry, with poorly concealed machineguns poking out of their clothing.
Perry dismissed a pledge by Iraq on Friday to abandon attacks on planes patrolling the Western-imposed zone, saying: "We cannot rely on Saddam Hussein's promises."
Asked if more U.S. strikes against Iraq were still possible, Perry said: "Yes, it is still a possibility."
Perry added he had ordered a battery of anti-missile Patriot missiles to Kuwait to strengthen its air defences.
Military sources say Kuwait over the past year has taken delivery of some of the hundreds of Patriots it ordered after the 1991 Gulf War but add these were not yet fully operational.
Perry also said he had asked Kuwait's emir, Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, for permission to proceed with a previously announced plan to deploy 5,000 U.S. troops in the Gulf state.
The emir had replied that Kuwait would say whether it would permit the deployment of the troops after the issue had been discussed by Kuwait's Supreme Defence Council, Perry said.
Perry said Saddam posed a danger not only in northern Iraq, where his forces attacked a Kurdish faction last month, but could also "move to coerce or even attack his neighbours to the south".

Perry, who arrived in Kuwait on Sunday after a short visit to neighbouring Saudi Arabia, also met Kuwait's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah and Defence Minister Sheikh Ahmad Hamoud al-Jaber al-Sabah at Kuwait international airport.
He later left and diplomats said they belived he was headed to Bahrain. Perry will also visit non-Arab regional ally Turkey.

Perry earlier on Sunday visited Saudi Arabia for talks with Saudi officials and also travelled to al-Kharg airbase 100 km (60 miles) southwest of the capital Riyadh to inspect security for U.S. forces stationed there.
Saudi Arabia, eager thus far not to appear as being directly involved in the current U.S. military buildup in the Gulf, has so far kept silent about Perry's visit.

Kuwait, grateful to Washington for leading the 1991 Gulf War that liberated it from a seven-month Iraqi occupation, is so far the only Arab country to support Washington in its latest standoff with Saddam.
But Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah said on Sunday there was no question of U.S. land forces crossing into Iraq from Kuwait.

"There is no passage for land forces, but there are air forces at Kuwaiti bases and this is not something new and they are also present in other states in the Gulf," he told reporters in the Egyptian city of Alexandria.
Eight Stealth bombers landed in Kuwait on Friday for a possible military strike against Iraq.
The Arab League, which groups all Arab states including Iraq and Washington's Gulf allies, condemned U.S. missile attacks on Iraq this month saying they violated Iraqi sovereignty.
While most of its regional allies are unwilling to take part, Washington has pressed on with the buildup in the region, including sending a second aircraft carrier battle group.
Perry defended the U.S. military buildup. "We believe it was necessary to take firm action," he said.
